ocar.opportunity: Textbook pictures of how proteins sit inside a cell are stitched together from biochemistry and electron microscopy. Directly seeing named proteins against whole-cell ultrastructure would test those pictures instead of assuming them.
ocar.challenge: Correlative super-resolution light and electron microscopy has traded off ultrastructure preservation, fluorescence retention, resolution, and field of view, so protein–ultrastructure maps have been incomplete or distorted.
ocar.action: Hoffman, Shtengel, Xu, and colleagues, in Science (2019; extract is the matching bioRxiv preprint), freeze fluorescently labeled cultured mammalian cells in vitreous ice, image them below 10 K by 3D SIM and SMLM, then image the same cells by FIB-SEM at 4- or 8-nm isotropic voxels and register the volumes.
ocar.resolution: The pipeline preserved native ultrastructure and revealed unexpected relationships: ER-marker-positive intranuclear vesicles, peroxisomes that become more irregular with size, highly convoluted endolysosomes, a web-like adhesion network between cultured cerebellar granule neurons, and chromatin domains subclassified by transcriptional-activity markers. Two-color cryo-SMLM registration was quantified to about 40 nm accuracy.
ocar.future_work: The discussion treats cryo-SR/FIB-SEM as a hypothesis generator and proposes combining it with cryo-EM tomography of FIB lamellae; automated segmentation of crowded intracellular features at terabyte scale remains the bottleneck named in the extract.

summaries.beginner: Seeing a named protein and the cell’s fine structure in the same whole cell is usually a compromise. This team freezes cells, images fluorescent labels, then mills the same cells with an electron microscope and finds several unexpected layouts, including a web of contacts between cultured brain cells.
summaries.intermediate: Hoffman and colleagues (Science, 2019; matching bioRxiv extract) combine cryogenic 3D structured illumination and single-molecule localization microscopy with focused-ion-beam scanning EM of entire vitreously frozen cultured mammalian cells. FIB-SEM is at 4- or 8-nm isotropic voxels; two-color cryo-SMLM registration is quantified to ~40 nm. Among reported surprises are ER-associated proteins in intranuclear vesicles, a web-like adhesion network between cerebellar granule neurons, and heterochromatin/euchromatin domains split by transcriptional-activity markers. Cryo-SIM, despite lower resolution, helped distinguish vesicles of similar EM morphology and aided segmentation in crowded cytoplasm.
summaries.advanced: The extract is the bioRxiv preprint of the Science paper (same title and authors), not the typeset journal PDF. Cells are cultured mammalian cells, not an intact brain volume. Counts such as 4- or 8-nm voxels and ~40 nm registration accuracy are those stated in the abstract/extract. Automated segmentation of 100 GB–scale (and larger) volumes is flagged as unsolved. Complementary cryo-ET of lamellae is proposed, not performed here.

plain_language_summary: Seeing a named protein and the cell’s fine structure in the same whole cell is usually a compromise. This team freezes cells, images fluorescent labels, then mills the same cells with an electron microscope and finds several unexpected layouts, including a web of contacts between cultured brain cells.

ocar.opportunity: Terabyte microscopy volumes now come with equally large integer label volumes. Interactive rendering and spatial queries need a fast way to ask which of millions of segments sit in a given region.
ocar.challenge: Integer labels are harder to store and randomly access than the raw images. Empty-space skipping and proximity queries over millions of IDs overwhelm conventional culling structures.
ocar.action: Beyer, Mohammed, Agus, Al-Awami, Pfister, and Hadwiger, in IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics (2019), introduce the label list tree: a data-adaptive hierarchy that stores, per node, either a probabilistic constant-time encoding for conservative culling or a deterministic logarithmic-time encoding for exact queries, plus a query-adaptive pruning strategy at run time.
ocar.resolution: Test volumes include connectomics label fields such as a mouse-cortex scan with more than 13 million labeled segments. The authors report significant reductions in storage and faster queries relative to conventional culling, with figures illustrating empty-space skipping and inter-segment distance queries.
ocar.future_work: The extract’s closing pages are references; claimed speed and size gains should be read from the paper’s result tables rather than treated as a single headline number.

summaries.beginner: Once every voxel in a huge brain image is given a label, even asking which objects sit where becomes slow. This paper stores those labels in a hybrid tree so viewers can skip empty space and run spatial queries over millions of segments.
summaries.intermediate: Beyer and colleagues (IEEE TVCG, 2019) target integer segmentation volumes from terabyte-scale microscopy. Their label list tree adaptively encodes each spatial node with either a probabilistic constant-time structure for conservative culling or a deterministic logarithmic-time structure for exact queries, and at run time further prunes queries down the tree. Datasets shown include Mouse Cortex 2 (13.25 million segments in a figure caption) and a brain scan with more than 13 million labeled segments in the abstract. The method is framed for empty-space skipping in volume rendering and for spatial proximity queries in connectomics proofreading and analysis.
summaries.advanced: This is a visualization/data-structure paper, not a new reconstruction. ‘Significant’ storage and query gains are qualitative in the abstract; the extract’s tail is references, so exact speedups should be taken from the full tables. Caption counts (13.25 million; 224,436 KESM mouse brain; 4.9 million phantom spheres; 4,107 SEM mouse cortex) describe example volumes, not a single benchmark score. Authorized IEEE Xplore copy.

plain_language_summary: Once every voxel in a huge brain image is given a label, even asking which objects sit where becomes slow. This paper stores those labels in a hybrid tree so viewers can skip empty space and run spatial queries over millions of segments.

ocar.opportunity: Connectomes give wiring without a full physiological census of every neuron. A theory that says which spike-timed computations a wiring diagram can or cannot support would turn maps into constraints on function.
ocar.challenge: It is unclear how far structure alone can go when high-level circuit function is unknown and detailed response properties are experimentally out of reach.
ocar.action: Ramaswamy, on bioRxiv (2019), extends an earlier axiomatic theory of connectomic constraints for feedforward deterministic spiking networks by studying the space of all spike-train-to-spike-train transformations, defining nested hierarchies of that space, and proving lower bounds on where architecture-limited transformation sets sit in those hierarchies.
ocar.resolution: The paper constructs explicit hierarchy classes and proves lower bounds for certain feedforward architectures. Neurons remain abstract objects obeying a few axioms rather than biophysically detailed cells. The stated use is to generate hypotheses from connectomic data and to compare architectures across individuals or species.
ocar.future_work: The extract emphasizes that exact hierarchy membership may be unattainable and that bounds are the realistic target; application to empirical connectomes is framed as a program, not a result of this preprint.

summaries.beginner: A wiring diagram does not automatically tell you what a circuit computes. This theory paper asks which timed spike computations a network could possibly perform, no matter how each neuron is tuned.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2019), Ramaswamy continues an axiomatic program on connectomic constraints for feedforward networks of deterministic spiking neurons. After prior work that asked which spike-timed computations can be ruled out from structure alone, this paper studies the space of spike-train-to-spike-train transformations, carves it into nested subsets defined by mathematical properties, and proves lower bounds relating those subsets to transformations spanned by specified architectures. The discussion flags uses in hypothesis generation from growing microscale maps and in comparative connectomics.
summaries.advanced: This is a theoretical preprint, not an empirical reconstruction. Bounds are for feedforward axiomatic neurons, not recurrent biophysical models. No numerical performance on a real connectome is reported in the extract. The author notes overlap with a University of Florida Ph.D. dissertation. Uncertified by peer review at posting.

plain_language_summary: A wiring diagram does not automatically tell you what a circuit computes. This theory paper asks which timed spike computations a network could possibly perform, no matter how each neuron is tuned.

ocar.opportunity: About 800 stereotyped medulla columns process the fly’s visual world. Specialized columns that detect polarized skylight should differ in cell types and synapses from ordinary color columns, if those differences can be mapped.
ocar.challenge: Cellular composition and synaptic wiring inside functionally specialized columns remain largely unknown, even as tools for morphology and connectivity have expanded.
ocar.action: Sancer, Kind, Plazaola, Balke, Pham, Hasan, Münch, Mathejczyk, and Wernet, on bioRxiv (2019), describe medulla circuitry downstream of dorsal-rim-area (DRA) photoreceptors, using anatomy plus activity-dependent GRASP and trans-Tango, and live imaging of pupal photoreceptor axons.
ocar.resolution: Only in DRA columns do both R7 and R8 target the bona fide R7 layer and contact previously uncharacterized Dm-DRA1 and Dm-DRA2 cells, which occupy separate sublayers and avoid color-sensitive Dm8. GRASP/trans-Tango place DRA R7→Dm-DRA1 and DRA R8→Dm-DRA2 synapses. R7 and R8 termini reach layer M6 sequentially in the pupa. The authors interpret this as a duplicated R7→Dm motif adapted for orthogonal e-vector analyzers.
ocar.future_work: How these medulla specializations continue into deeper navigation centers is outside the extract; the piece is a circuit-anatomy preprint, not a volume-EM connectome of the whole optic lobe.

summaries.beginner: Flies use a strip of eye at the top of the head to sense the sky’s polarized light. This study shows that those specialized pixels wire to their own partner cells in the next brain layer, separate from the cells that handle color.
summaries.intermediate: Sancer and colleagues (bioRxiv, 2019) map medulla columns downstream of Drosophila dorsal-rim-area photoreceptors. In DRA columns only, R7 and R8 both terminate in the R7 target layer onto two DRA-specific Dm types (Dm-DRA1 and Dm-DRA2) that stratify in separate sublayers and do not overlap color-sensitive Dm8. Activity-dependent GRASP and trans-Tango support DRA R7–Dm-DRA1 and DRA R8–Dm-DRA2 synapses. Live imaging shows the two photoreceptor classes reach layer M6 in sequence. The optic lobe is described as ~800 retinotopic columnar microcircuits; DRA ommatidia are treated as orthogonal UV e-vector analyzers that are necessary and sufficient for polarized-light orientation in walking flies (as cited from prior work).
summaries.advanced: This is a bioRxiv preprint using genetic anatomy, GRASP, trans-Tango, and live imaging, not a dense EM reconstruction. Synaptic claims are those of the activity-dependent methods named in the abstract. The ~800-column figure is the standard optic-lobe count stated in the abstract. Sequential arrival at M6 is a developmental observation, not a full wiring diagram of downstream polarotactic pathways.

plain_language_summary: Flies use a strip of eye at the top of the head to sense the sky’s polarized light. This study shows that those specialized pixels wire to their own partner cells in the next brain layer, separate from the cells that handle color.

ocar.opportunity: Modulatory neurons supply teaching signals for associative learning, but the synaptic circuits that compute those signals are poorly mapped. A complete upstream connectome of a compact learning center would show how memories of opposite valence can interact.
ocar.challenge: How prior memories, context, and opposite-valence compartments jointly set dopaminergic teaching signals remains unclear in both insects and vertebrates.
ocar.action: Eschbach, Fushiki, Winding, Schneider-Mizell, Shao, Arruda, Eichler, Valdes-Aleman, Ohyama, Thum, Gerber, Fetter, Truman, Litwin-Kumar, Cardona, and Zlatic, on bioRxiv (2019), reconstruct synaptic-resolution circuitry upstream of all modulatory neurons in the Drosophila larval mushroom body, test some pathways functionally, and simulate a connectome-constrained learning model.
ocar.resolution: They report afferent sensory paths plus 61 feedback neuron pairs providing one- and two-step feedback from mushroom-body output neurons, most linking distinct memory systems. Some modulatory neurons appear to compare inhibition from their own compartment with excitation from opposite-valence compartments. The model indicates that multilevel feedback and cross-compartment connections increase performance and flexibility on learning tasks.
ocar.future_work: The extract’s discussion treats the map as a basis for circuit implementations of prediction-error and common-currency value; not all 61 pairs are functionally confirmed, and adult mushroom-body generality is not claimed here.

summaries.beginner: Learning signals in the fly larva’s memory center are not a simple one-way drip of dopamine. This team maps every incoming synapse onto those signal cells and finds a large web of feedback that lets old memories of good and bad change what is learned next.
summaries.intermediate: Eschbach, Fushiki, Winding, Schneider-Mizell and colleagues (bioRxiv, 2019) present a synaptic-resolution connectome of neurons upstream of all modulatory neurons in the Drosophila larval mushroom body. They report sensory afferents and an unexpected 61 pairs of feedback neurons providing one- and two-step feedback from mushroom-body output neurons, mostly bridging aversive and appetitive compartments. Functional tests indicate that some modulatory neurons combine own-compartment inhibition with opposite-valence excitation. A model constrained by the connectome and those data is used to argue that multilevel feedback and cross-compartment links improve computational performance and flexibility on learning tasks.
summaries.advanced: This is a bioRxiv preprint (May 2019 posting in the extract), later published in a journal; summaries follow this extract. The ‘first’ claim is the authors’ for this larval MB upstream circuit. The count of 61 feedback neuron pairs is from the abstract. Functional confirmation is partial (‘some’ pathways). Model performance gains are qualitative in the extract (figures 7a–e), not a single accuracy number. EM reconstruction is of the larval mushroom-body teaching circuit, not the whole larval CNS.

plain_language_summary: Learning signals in the fly larva’s memory center are not a simple one-way drip of dopamine. This team maps every incoming synapse onto those signal cells and finds a large web of feedback that lets old memories of good and bad change what is learned next.

ocar.opportunity: Müller glia are the first retinal cells to change in degeneration, so a pathoconnectome that places one reconstructed Müller cell among neighboring neurons and glia could link metabolic state to ultrastructure.
ocar.challenge: How Müller-cell metabolic chaos relates to neuronal stress, synapse maintenance, or glia–glia contacts in early remodeling is unknown.
ocar.action: Pfeiffer, Anderson, Emrich, Dahal, Sigulinsky, Morrison, Yang, Watt, Rapp, Kondo, Terasaki, Garcia, Marc, and Jones, in Advances in Experimental Medicine and Biology (2019), reconstruct a Müller cell from retinal pathoconnectome 1 (RPC1) and compare ultrastructure with computational molecular phenotyping of small-molecule metabolites.
ocar.resolution: They report intra- and intercellular variation in osmication, variable glutamine and taurine content across Müller cells unlike the homogeneous pattern in normal retina, and increased branching and intertwining of Müller endfeet in early remodeling (described as a morphology not normally found in rabbit retinas). RPC1 is presented as a framework for neuron–glia analysis in early retinal degeneration.
ocar.future_work: The chapter’s conclusion calls for continued analysis of Müller interactions with neurons and glia, and of how entanglement affects metabolic exchange; whether glutamine/taurine states are stable or metastable is left open.

summaries.beginner: When the retina starts to degenerate, support cells called Müller glia change first. This short study reconstructs one such cell in a diseased-retina wiring volume and shows mixed chemistry and tangled endfeet even at an early stage.
summaries.intermediate: Pfeiffer and colleagues (Adv. Exp. Med. Biol., 2019) reconstruct a Müller cell from retinal pathoconnectome 1 (RPC1) of early remodeling, combining serial ultrastructure with computational molecular phenotyping. They find variable osmication within and between Müller cells, heterogeneous small-molecule (glutamine and taurine) labels compared with homogeneous healthy retina, and hypertrophic endfeet with extra branching and intertwining. The extract links the endfoot change to the start of chaotic glial entanglement described by Fisher and Lewis. The work is a book-chapter progress report, not a complete pathoconnectome census.
summaries.advanced: PMC author manuscript of a short chapter (pages 365–370). Species context in the extract includes rabbit retina for the endfoot morphology claim. Q and τ refer to glutamine and taurine immunoreactivity. GS (glutamine synthetase) variation is mentioned as data not shown. No synapse counts or complete cell census appear in the extract. Lipid species driving osmication variability are unknown.

plain_language_summary: When the retina starts to degenerate, support cells called Müller glia change first. This short study reconstructs one such cell in a diseased-retina wiring volume and shows mixed chemistry and tangled endfeet even at an early stage.

ocar.opportunity: Complete 3-D shapes of long-projecting mammalian neurons are a cell-type gold standard, but they sit in tens of teravoxels of whole-brain imagery that 2-D screens and mice handle poorly.
ocar.challenge: Validating full-morphology reconstructions is laborious, and existing tools struggle with fine distal arbors in whole-brain volumes.
ocar.action: Wang, Li, Liu, Zhou, Ruan, Kong, Li, Wang, Zhong, Chai, Luo, Guo, Hawrylycz, Luo, Gu, Xie, Zeng, and Peng, in Nature Communications (2019), introduce TeraVR, an open-source VR annotation system with immersive collaborative 3-D visualization, interaction, and hierarchical streaming of teravoxel-scale images.
ocar.resolution: Using TeraVR they report precise full 3-D morphologies of long-projecting neurons in whole mouse brains and a collaborative workflow for highly accurate reconstruction. Discussion highlights remote co-curation and optional AI tracing modules (DeepNeuron, SmartTracing) as distinctive features.
ocar.future_work: The authors suggest applying the same streaming/VR stack to light-sheet, expansion, and lattice microscopy volumes and using AI for integrity checks; those uses are proposed, not benchmarked as the main result.

summaries.beginner: Tracing a neuron across an entire mouse brain is like following a thread through a warehouse of images. This team puts the volume in virtual reality so people can walk the branches together and finish complete 3-D shapes.
summaries.intermediate: Wang and colleagues (Nature Communications, 2019) present TeraVR, an open-source virtual-reality system for annotating neurons in teravoxel whole-brain images. It combines immersive 3-D visualization, hierarchical streaming, and a collaborative mode in which remote users curate one another’s reconstructions. The authors report precise full morphologies of long-projecting neurons in whole mouse brains. Discussion argues that no prior open-source VR package handled this class of whole-brain imagery and that 2-D displays make overlaying geometry on volume data awkward.
summaries.advanced: This is a methods/software paper; ‘precise’ and ‘highly accurate’ are the authors’ claims without a single numeric error rate in the extract. Reconstructions are light-microscopy whole-brain morphologies, not synaptic EM connectomes. AI integration (DeepNeuron, SmartTracing) is discussed as an extension. Data-availability mentions NeuroMorpho.Org and BICCN releases in the extract’s discussion.

plain_language_summary: Tracing a neuron across an entire mouse brain is like following a thread through a warehouse of images. This team puts the volume in virtual reality so people can walk the branches together and finish complete 3-D shapes.

ocar.opportunity: Synapses are molecularly diverse, but there was no whole-brain, single-synapse map of that diversity. Such a synaptome could be compared with structural and functional connectomes and with disease mutations.
ocar.challenge: Light and electron microscopy of synapses have been limited to small fields, so the spatial logic of synapse types across the mouse brain was unknown.
ocar.action: Zhu, Cizeron, Qiu, Benavides-Piccione, Kopanitsa, Skene, Koniaris, DeFelipe, Fransén, Komiyama, and Grant, in Neuron (2018), genetically label postsynaptic proteins and image individual excitatory synapses across mouse-brain regions, building catalogs from molecular and morphological features.
ocar.resolution: The abstract reports catalogs from a billion synapses, unique anatomical distributions per subtype, region-specific subtype signatures, correspondence with structural and functional connectomes, greatest diversity in higher cognitive areas, and reorganization of synaptome maps by mutations that cause cognitive disorders. Behaviorally relevant activity patterns are said to trigger postsynaptic responses that depend on synaptome structure.
ocar.future_work: Resources (Synaptome Explorer, maps, and puncta tables) are released for further studies of normal and diseased brain; the extract’s tail is software/data availability rather than a new experimental series.

summaries.beginner: Brain maps usually count cells or cables, not the molecular flavors of individual synapses. This mouse atlas labels excitatory synapses across the whole brain and finds that each region has its own mix, which disease mutations can scramble.
summaries.intermediate: Zhu and colleagues (Neuron, 2018) map postsynaptic proteins at single excitatory synapses across the mouse brain using genetic labeling and imaging. From molecular and morphological features they generate catalogs described as covering a billion synapses, with each subtype showing a unique anatomical distribution and each region a distinct subtype signature. Highlights include single-synapse-resolution maps of postsynaptic proteins, correspondence between synapse diversity and structural/functional connectomes, highest diversity in areas linked to higher cognition, and reorganization of maps by disease-relevant mutations. Accompanying software (Synaptome Explorer) visualizes individual puncta on delineated sections.
summaries.advanced: ‘A billion synapses’ and ‘billions of individual synapses across 5 coronal sections’ are the paper’s stated scales; they are not an EM synapse census. The map is of labeled excitatory postsynaptic puncta (PSD95/SAP102 in the data section), not a complete proteome of all synapse classes. Electrophysiological arguments about activity patterns are from modeling referenced in the data tables. Europe PMC HTML/PDF extract.

plain_language_summary: Brain maps usually count cells or cables, not the molecular flavors of individual synapses. This mouse atlas labels excitatory synapses across the whole brain and finds that each region has its own mix, which disease mutations can scramble.

ocar.opportunity: C. elegans has a complete connectome but still needs a mechanistic account of who generates the undulatory motor rhythm. Locating oscillators in identified motor neurons would compress rhythm generation, proprioception, and descending control into a tiny circuit.
ocar.challenge: Classic central-pattern-generator pictures assume bursting interneurons; worm body undulation may instead ride on non-bursting ventral-cord excitatory motor neurons whose coupling is proprioceptive.
ocar.action: Wen, Gao, and Zhen, in Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B (2018), review recent physiology and genetics arguing that A-class and mid-body B-class excitatory ventral-cord motor neurons act as intrinsic oscillators for reversal and forward undulation, respectively, with proprioception phase-coupling members of each class and premotor interneurons modulating and coupling them.
ocar.resolution: They propose two motor sub-circuits of oscillators plus descending inputs as the structural basis for switching forward and backward states. Integrating rhythm generation and proprioception into motor neurons, and descending regulation into premotor interneurons, is presented as circuit-level functional compression analogous to more complex motor systems.
ocar.future_work: The piece sits in a ‘Connectome to behaviour’ discussion issue and frames a continuing program toward a dynamic sensorimotor model rather than a new reconstruction.

summaries.beginner: The worm’s crawling wave has to start somewhere in its tiny nervous system. This review argues that the motor neurons themselves keep time, while stretch sensing and a few command cells keep the wave traveling the right way.
summaries.intermediate: Wen, Gao, and Zhen (Phil. Trans. R. Soc. B, 2018) review evidence that C. elegans A-class and mid-body B-class excitatory ventral-cord motor neurons function as non-bursting intrinsic oscillators for backward and forward body undulation. Proprioception is argued to entrain those oscillators and phase-couple cells of the same class so undulations propagate. Distinct premotor interneuron pools innervate all members of each class, modulating oscillations and promoting bidirectional coupling. The authors treat this as functional compression: rhythm generation and proprioception in motor neurons, descending control in premotor interneurons. The article is part of a discussion meeting issue on modelling C. elegans at cellular resolution.
summaries.advanced: This is a review plus discussion of prior findings, not a new EM volume. Oscillator assignments are proposals based on cited physiology (including ablation experiments described in the methods notes for figures). The extract includes experimental-methods fragments for unc-2 and miniSOG ablation of A-class cells from the authors’ related work. No new synapse counts are introduced here.

plain_language_summary: The worm’s crawling wave has to start somewhere in its tiny nervous system. This review argues that the motor neurons themselves keep time, while stretch sensing and a few command cells keep the wave traveling the right way.

ocar.opportunity: Unlike the rest of the body, the C. elegans snout can move in all directions, which likely matters for navigating a 3-D soil matrix. Head somatotopy in the connectome is a clue to how that extra freedom is wired.
ocar.challenge: Locomotory waves are confined to one dorso-ventral plane, so models built only on body locomotion miss the snout’s degrees of freedom.
ocar.action: White, in Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B (2018), contrasts body versus snout muscle innervation: shared dorsal and ventral quadrant innervation along the body versus an octagonal innervation of snout muscles, and argues that octant-specific motor, sensory, and interneurons mediate exploratory head movements.
ocar.resolution: The well-defined anatomy and circuitry, together with behavioral observation, are presented as sufficient to start models of this relatively complex exploratory behaviour, with analogies to vertebrate foraging. Circuits of motor and receptor neurons for four of six labia are described as similar and tentatively split into functional units.
ocar.future_work: White notes that head movements have been observed far less than locomotion and taxis, and sketches 3-D imaging, magnetic-bead stimuli to single labia, and connectome-constrained simulations as next steps.

summaries.beginner: A worm crawls by bending in one plane, but the tip of its head can poke around in all directions. This essay reads the head’s wiring diagram as an eight-sided steering system for exploring soil.
summaries.intermediate: White (Phil. Trans. R. Soc. B, 2018) reviews C. elegans snout versus body motor innervation. Body muscle uses common innervation of the two dorsal quadrants and of the two ventral quadrants, matching planar undulation, whereas snout muscles have an octagonal innervation likely served by octant-specific motor and sensory neurons plus associated interneurons. Exploratory snout movements are linked to seeking passages in a 3-D soil matrix. The article is part of the same ‘Connectome to behaviour’ issue and is a perspective built on existing anatomy rather than new reconstructions.
summaries.advanced: This is a single-author review/perspective. Octagonal innervation and labial circuit similarity are anatomical arguments, not new EM. Proposed 3-D tracking and magnetic-bead assays are suggestions. Neuron count 302 is mentioned in passing as background. Europe PMC copy.

plain_language_summary: A worm crawls by bending in one plane, but the tip of its head can poke around in all directions. This essay reads the head’s wiring diagram as an eight-sided steering system for exploring soil.

ocar.opportunity: Eigenvectors of a network already highlight central vertices. Extending them to communities tied to those vertices could read information-flow structure from a static connectome without simulating dynamics.
ocar.challenge: Community detection often ignores directed flow, and some have claimed that hubs such as hippocampus cannot be recovered from static graphs.
ocar.action: Clark and Macdonald, on bioRxiv (2018), define eigenvector-based communities, each associated with a prominent vertex, and apply the method to C. elegans, macaque, and a large-scale human MRI connectome of about 1.8 million vertices.
ocar.resolution: In C. elegans, known circuitry appears as separate communities. In macaque, the hippocampus is recovered as an information hub. In humans, prominent pathways from a scan are used as a subject identifier by counting matching pathways between connectomes, including scan–rescan comparison in a twenty-subject dataset named in the discussion.
ocar.future_work: The authors stress that undirected MRI graphs cannot distinguish sources from sinks and that Laplacian analysis of directed graphs would be more informative; cognitive-change tracking via pathway turnover is proposed, not demonstrated as a clinical tool.

summaries.beginner: Some brain regions are hubs that gather or send lots of signals. This methods preprint uses the math of network eigenvectors to find those hubs and their neighborhoods in worm, monkey, and human connection maps.
summaries.intermediate: Clark and Macdonald (bioRxiv, 2018) use multiple eigenvectors to define communities, each anchored on a prominent vertex that is a major source or destination of network flow. Applied to C. elegans, the method recovers known circuits as separate communities. Applied to macaque (CoCoMac), it identifies hippocampus as an information hub, which the authors contrast with claims that static graphs cannot yield that insight. On a human connectome of ~1.8 million vertices they extract prominent pathways and argue that matching pathways can identify a subject across scans. Discussion notes that undirected MRI networks hide in/out imbalance.
summaries.advanced: bioRxiv preprint. C. elegans is a nematode; the extract’s ‘flatworm’ wording in the author summary is a taxonomic slip and should not be repeated as fact. The ~1.8 million-vertex figure and twenty-subject Landmann et al. scan–rescan claim are the authors’. Hippocampus-as-hub is a graph-analytic result on CoCoMac, not new tracing. Human application is MRI-scale, not synaptic EM.

plain_language_summary: Some brain regions are hubs that gather or send lots of signals. This methods preprint uses the math of network eigenvectors to find those hubs and their neighborhoods in worm, monkey, and human connection maps.

ocar.opportunity: Connectomic EM volumes are too large for manual mitochondrial census, yet mitochondrial morphology and occupancy matter for disease and for distinguishing inhibitory versus excitatory neurites.
ocar.challenge: Mitochondria vary in shape and sectioning angle; existing EPFL Hippocampus labels have boundary errors; and detectors must outrun single-beam SEM acquisition (~11 megapixels/s) to be usable online.
ocar.action: Casser, Kang, Pfister, and Haehn (arXiv 1812.06024; MIDL 2020 extract titled Fast Mitochondria Detection for Connectomics) train a modified 2D U-Net, re-annotate Lucchi’s EPFL Hippocampus data as Lucchi++ and Kasthuri mitochondria as Kasthuri++, and benchmark against prior detectors.
ocar.resolution: They report Jaccard/IoU up to 0.90 (abstract) and IoU in the range 0.845–0.90 with average inference about 16 ms per 512×512 tile, faster than modern EM acquisition, ranking first among real-time methods and third overall. Code and the two re-annotated benchmarks are released.
ocar.future_work: The method is 2D to avoid expensive pre-alignment; 3D context and remaining ranking versus slower high-accuracy methods are left to comparison tables in the full paper.

summaries.beginner: Mitochondria in electron-microscope brain images are clues to cell health, but there are far too many to outline by hand. This detector outlines them as fast as the microscope can scan, using a compact neural net.
summaries.intermediate: Casser, Kang, Pfister, and Haehn (arXiv 1812.06024v2 / MIDL 2020) present a 2D U-Net-style mitochondria detector for connectomic EM. They release Lucchi++, a re-annotation of the EPFL Hippocampus benchmark by three experts, and Kasthuri++, a similarly cleaned neocortex set. Reported accuracy is a Jaccard index up to 0.90 and IoU 0.845–0.90, with inference below 16 ms (abstract) or about 16 ms average (results paragraph) per 512×512 tile, intended to beat ~11 megapixels/s single-beam SEM. The catalog title says ‘Segmentation’; the extract title says ‘Detection’—same paper.
summaries.advanced: Catalog title is Fast Mitochondria Segmentation; the PDF extract is the MIDL 2020 version titled Fast Mitochondria Detection (same arXiv id and authors). Jaccard 0.90 and 16 ms are the authors’ headline numbers; IoU 0.845–0.90 is the range in the results paragraph. Ranking first among real-time methods and third overall is their comparison claim. Not a synaptic reconstruction. uuid is the work_id because the catalog record has no DOI.

plain_language_summary: Mitochondria in electron-microscope brain images are clues to cell health, but there are far too many to outline by hand. This detector outlines them as fast as the microscope can scan, using a compact neural net.

ocar.opportunity: A functional connectome that captures how stimuli propagate could complement the anatomical C. elegans wiring diagram, especially for behaviours whose pathways are only partly known.
ocar.challenge: Direct inference on a full neuronal dynamical system is intractable; pairwise dependencies in high-dimensional time series need a compact graphical representation.
ocar.action: Liu, Kim, and Shlizerman, in Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B (2018), collect simulated neuronal time series, project them with SVD, extract dominant pairwise dependencies, and build a probabilistic graphical model of the C. elegans somatic nervous-system model.
ocar.resolution: The resulting PGM is presented as a functional connectome of causal dependencies among neurons and stimuli. Applied to an existing dynamical model of the worm soma, it recovers pathways for known behavioural scenarios and suggests pathways for novel ones.
ocar.future_work: The extract’s visible body is largely methods and a small example network; generalization from the simulated soma model to in vivo recordings is the implied next step, not shown here.

summaries.beginner: The worm’s wiring diagram is known, but activity still has to travel along it. This paper turns simulated neuron traces into a probability map of who depends on whom when a stimulus arrives.
summaries.intermediate: Liu, Kim, and Shlizerman (Phil. Trans. R. Soc. B, 2018) convert neuronal time series into a probabilistic graphical model. They SVD-project the traces, extract dominant pairwise dependencies, and assemble a graph whose edges are treated as causal stimulus-propagation routes. They apply the pipeline to a published dynamical model of the C. elegans somatic nervous system (gap junctions and chemical synapses in the extract’s equations) to recover known behavioural pathways and propose ones for new scenarios. The article is part of the ‘Connectome to behaviour’ issue.
summaries.advanced: This is method plus application to a simulated soma model, not new EM or calcium imaging. ‘Causal’ is the authors’ interpretation of the PGM. The extract’s end is dominated by Jacobian/conditional-probability worked examples rather than a full pathway catalog. Conditional probabilities in the toy example include a negative value mapped to 0, underscoring that the visible extract is methodological.

plain_language_summary: The worm’s wiring diagram is known, but activity still has to travel along it. This paper turns simulated neuron traces into a probability map of who depends on whom when a stimulus arrives.

ocar.opportunity: Presynaptic transmission is energy-hungry and calcium-sensitive, and mitochondria are built for both jobs. Understanding why some boutons have mitochondria and others do not would clarify computation and disease risk at the synapse.
ocar.challenge: Not all presynapses contain mitochondria, trafficking rules are incomplete, and extra roles beyond ATP and calcium buffering are still being enumerated.
ocar.action: Devine and Kittler, in Nature Reviews Neuroscience (2018), review trafficking of mitochondria to presynapses, ATP supply and Ca2+ buffering during transmission, additional presynaptic roles, and links to neurodegenerative disease.
ocar.resolution: They emphasize active recruitment of mitochondria, motile fractions and speeds reported from cultured neurons in the extract (10–20% of axonal mitochondria motile at 0.2–2 μm/s in cultured hippocampal neurons), and argue that occupancy may buy computational flexibility while signalling and ER interactions also matter. Disease discussion focuses on neurodegeneration.
ocar.future_work: The conclusion calls for genetically encoded reporters of mitochondrial position, calcium, and vesicle release in vivo, plus transgenic and iPSC disease models, to pin down how mutations break the chain from mitochondria to synapses to neurons.

summaries.beginner: Nerve terminals need energy and tight calcium control, jobs mitochondria are good at, yet many terminals have none. This review asks what mitochondria do at the sending side of a synapse and how their failure might lead to disease.
summaries.intermediate: Devine and Kittler (Nature Reviews Neuroscience, 2018) survey presynaptic mitochondria. They review nuclear-encoded biogenesis, axonal trafficking, ATP production and Ca2+ buffering during vesicle release, and additional roles including biosynthesis and ER interaction. The extract cites 10–20% motile axonal mitochondria in cultured hippocampal neurons at 0.2–2 μm/s. They ask why some presynapses lack mitochondria and how dysfunction contributes to neurodegeneration. Future work highlighted is real-time in vivo reporters plus disease models.
summaries.advanced: This is a narrative review (UCL accepted-manuscript extract), not original connectomic mapping. Motility percentages and speeds are cited from the literature in the extract, not new measurements. Disease mechanisms are discussed as incompletely defined. Figure 1 and later sections are not fully present in the supplied extract.

plain_language_summary: Nerve terminals need energy and tight calcium control, jobs mitochondria are good at, yet many terminals have none. This review asks what mitochondria do at the sending side of a synapse and how their failure might lead to disease.

ocar.opportunity: From fly to human, brain-region graphs show wiring-cost and homophily plus modules and hubs. A developmental mechanism using only space and time could explain those regularities without invoking plasticity or guidance-cue maps.
ocar.challenge: The processes that produce heterogeneous interregional strengths and global topology are unknown; cost-minimization descriptions do not by themselves supply a growth rule.
ocar.action: Goulas, Betzel, and Hilgetag, in Science Advances (2019 version of a 2018-catalogued paper), computationally grow connectomes from heterochronous, spatially ordered neurodevelopmental gradients with stochastic axonal growth and no activity-dependent plasticity or axonal guidance cues, then compare synthetic graphs to adult fly and vertebrate connectomes.
ocar.resolution: They report reconstructing on average 83% of wiring-principle structure and 80% of global network topology across diverse adult connectomes, including fly and human. Heterochronous, spatially ordered ontogeny is said to occupy a different topology morphospace from tautochronous growth and to resemble Drosophila, mouse, macaque, and human brains.
ocar.future_work: Activity-dependent refinement is acknowledged as a later sculptor. Pathologies of Notch/BMP timing are suggested as routes to deviant large-scale topology; those links are interpretive.

summaries.beginner: Brains of flies and humans look different but share cheap, cliquey wiring and a few hubs. This model grows those patterns from staggered developmental clocks and spatial position, without needing learning or chemical trail maps.
summaries.intermediate: Goulas, Betzel, and Hilgetag (Science Advances, 2019) model interregional connectomes as the outcome of heterochronous, spatially ordered neurodevelopmental gradients plus stochastic axon growth. Without activity-dependent plasticity or guidance-cue gradients, the model is reported to recover on average 83% of wiring-cost/homophily principles and 80% of global topology (modules, hubs) for adult connectomes ranging from fly to human. Discussion treats space and time as a potentially universal, parsimonious ontogenetic mechanism and notes that mammalian and insect brains both show the same descriptive principles empirically.
summaries.advanced: Percentages (83%, 80%) are ‘on average’ claims from the abstract; species-wise breakdowns live in figures not fully quoted in the extract. This is computational modeling of region-scale connectomes, not synaptic EM. Catalog year is 2018; the PDF is the 2019 Science Advances article (same title/authors). Guidance cues and plasticity are omitted by design, not shown to be biologically absent.

plain_language_summary: Brains of flies and humans look different but share cheap, cliquey wiring and a few hubs. This model grows those patterns from staggered developmental clocks and spatial position, without needing learning or chemical trail maps.

ocar.opportunity: A complete worm connectome still needs a body: sensors and muscles only make sense if the physical animal is modeled. A 3-D biomechanical body would let neural activity be tested as movement.
ocar.challenge: Prior models often under-represent cuticle, hydrostatic skeleton, and anatomically placed muscle cells in liquid versus gel.
ocar.action: Palyanov, Khayrulin, and Larson, in Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B (2018), build a particle-based C. elegans body in Sibernetic (smoothed particle hydrodynamics) with an elastic cuticle under hydrostatic pressure and body-wall muscles mapped from light microscopy and electron micrographs.
ocar.resolution: Different muscle-activation patterns produce crawling- and swimming-like locomotion in environments of different viscosity while matching multiple known biomechanical properties. The engine is presented as extensible to pharynx, egg-laying, and defecation musculature.
ocar.future_work: Coupling this body to a full neural model and adding more organs are named next steps; the paper does not itself close the loop from connectome to behaviour.

summaries.beginner: To know whether a worm’s nerve cells explain crawling, you need a virtual body that can bend in water or on gel. This simulation gives the animal a physical skin and muscles copied from anatomy.
summaries.intermediate: Palyanov, Khayrulin, and Larson (Phil. Trans. R. Soc. B, 2018) present a 3-D C. elegans body model in the Sibernetic SPH engine. An elastic body-wall cuticle under hydrostatic pressure is driven by anatomically placed body-wall muscle cells derived from light microscopy and EM. Varied activation patterns yield crawling- and swimming-like behaviour in different viscosities and are said to fit additional known biomechanics. The article is part of the OpenWorm-linked ‘Connectome to behaviour’ issue. Video links in the extract illustrate swimming, crawling, reversal, omega turns, and shortening.
summaries.advanced: This is a biomechanical body model, not a new connectome. Muscle positions come from published anatomy/EM, not a new volume. Quantitative error versus real kinematics should be taken from the full figures; the abstract says the model fits ‘multiple additional known biomechanical properties’ without listing numbers in the extract. Neural control is an input pattern, not a simulated nervous system.

plain_language_summary: To know whether a worm’s nerve cells explain crawling, you need a virtual body that can bend in water or on gel. This simulation gives the animal a physical skin and muscles copied from anatomy.

ocar.opportunity: Mouse LGN is a small, well-studied visual thalamic hub that is now a standard model, yet its feedforward/feedback mix, channel interactions, and developmental rewiring are still poorly mapped at synapse scale.
ocar.challenge: Connection probability is usually treated as cell type plus proximity, which hides higher-order motifs that only intact network reconstructions can show.
ocar.action: Morgan, in Visual Neuroscience (2017), reviews why circuit-scale electron microscopy (cellular connectomics) can reconstruct synaptic connectivity of hundreds of neurons in a volume the size of mouse LGN, yielding both cell-type wiring diagrams and higher-order motifs.
ocar.resolution: The piece argues that LGN connectomics can answer longstanding questions about visual thalamus and mammalian circuit formation. It is a short special-collection review, not a new reconstruction.
ocar.future_work: The implied program is to apply then-emerging EM segmentation and reconstruction methods to mouse LGN; no new dataset is released here.

summaries.beginner: The brain’s visual relay station is small enough that a modern electron-microscope volume could hold hundreds of its neurons. This short review explains why mapping every synapse there would settle old arguments about how vision is wired.
summaries.intermediate: Morgan (Visual Neuroscience, 2017) writes a five-page review on a connectomic approach to the lateral geniculate nucleus. Core LGN function is described as well understood, while feedforward/feedback integration, cross-channel interactions, and activity-dependent restructuring remain open—especially in mouse, despite its status as a model. Circuit-scale EM is presented as able to reconstruct synaptic connectivity of hundreds of neurons in a mouse-LGN-sized volume, exposing canonical cell-type wiring and higher-order motifs. The article is an Open Access special-collection review (Visual Thalamus), not an empirical volume.
summaries.advanced: No new reconstructions, synapse counts, or EM figures of mouse LGN are in this paper. ‘Hundreds of neurons’ is a capability claim for then-current cellular connectomics, not a completed map. Cambridge University Press HTML/PDF extract.

plain_language_summary: The brain’s visual relay station is small enough that a modern electron-microscope volume could hold hundreds of its neurons. This short review explains why mapping every synapse there would settle old arguments about how vision is wired.

ocar.opportunity: Electron tomograms contain thousands of synaptic vesicles whose size and pool statistics matter in development and mutants, but manual IMOD tracing does not scale.
ocar.challenge: Vesicles must be separated from other round densities; fully automatic detectors trade precision for recall; learning-based tools still need heavy supervision.
ocar.action: Kaltdorf, Schulze, Helmprobst, Kollmannsberger, Dandekar, and Stigloher, in PLoS Computational Biology (2017), release Fiji macros (3D ART VeSElecT) that preprocess 1 nm/pixel stacks, segment vesicles in 3-D, measure inner/outer diameter and volume, and optionally let users prune false positives in RoiManager.
ocar.resolution: On zebrafish NMJ they report smaller vesicles at 8 dpf than at 4 dpf, matching manual reconstruction. They also compare C. elegans N2 NMJ with septin mutant unc-59(e261). Speed gain versus manual annotation is stated as up to 68-fold, with small error rates; precision/recall are tunable via volume, sphericity, and elongation filters.
ocar.future_work: The macros are aimed at prescreening and developmental or mutant screens; generalization beyond round vesicles in tomograms is not the claim.

summaries.beginner: Counting synaptic bubbles in 3-D electron-microscope movies by hand is painfully slow. This Fiji toolkit finds the bubbles automatically, with an optional human cleanup step, and is used on fish and worm synapses.
summaries.intermediate: Kaltdorf and colleagues (PLoS Computational Biology, 2017) describe 3D ART VeSElecT, two Fiji macros for registering and measuring synaptic vesicles in electron tomograms. Input stacks are 1 nm/pixel in x and y. They quantify zebrafish neuromuscular-junction vesicles at 4 versus 8 days post-fertilization (smaller at 8 dpf, validated manually) and C. elegans wild-type versus unc-59(e261) septin-mutant NMJs. Compared with manual IMOD tracing the authors report up to 68× speedup and few errors, with optional manual filtering and gains versus ilastik in segmentation/filtering. User constraints (volume, sphericity, elongation) trade recall against precision.
summaries.advanced: ‘Up to 68 times faster’ is the authors’ headline; it is not a mean across all datasets. Vesicle diameters in the extract are not given as a single pair of numbers in the abstract beyond the qualitative 8 dpf < 4 dpf result. The tool assumes approximately spherical vesicles. Code URL is given in the extract. This is vesicle morphometry, not a synaptic-connectivity map.

plain_language_summary: Counting synaptic bubbles in 3-D electron-microscope movies by hand is painfully slow. This Fiji toolkit finds the bubbles automatically, with an optional human cleanup step, and is used on fish and worm synapses.

ocar.opportunity: Identified modulatory neurons are often treated as uniform top-down broadcast. Mapping every synaptic class onto a pair of identified serotonergic cells would show whether they listen to the network they modulate.
ocar.challenge: Modulatory populations are heterogeneous in physiology, anatomy, and genes, so principles of individual-neuron connectivity are hard to extract.
ocar.action: Coates, Majot, Zhang, Michael, Spitzer, Gaudry, and Dacks, in Journal of Neuroscience (2017), use anatomical methods in Drosophila to map inputs onto the paired CSDns in the antennal lobe and to count CSDn active zones across glomeruli.
ocar.resolution: CSDns receive glomerulus-specific input from olfactory receptor neurons and projection neurons and network-wide input from local interneurons. Their output active zones are heterogeneous across glomeruli yet stereotyped across animals. They synapse onto LNs and PNs throughout the AL but not onto ORNs. Modulation is therefore not purely top-down, and even a two-cell serotonergic system has structured, nonreciprocal connectivity.
ocar.future_work: Functional consequences of sparse ORN drive (e.g., ammonia via Ir92a/VM1) are tied to prior physiology; expanding from this pair to other modulators is left open.

summaries.beginner: Brain chemicals that change mood-like states are often imagined as a sprinkler system. In the fly nose, two serotonin cells both listen to and speak to specific odor channels, not uniformly.
summaries.intermediate: Coates and colleagues (Journal of Neuroscience, 2017) map connectivity of the paired Drosophila CSDns in the antennal lobe. Anatomical methods show glomerulus-specific ORN and PN input, widespread LN input, and CSDn output onto LNs and PNs but not ORNs. Active-zone counts are heterogeneous across glomeruli and stereotyped between animals. Discussion links sparse ORN synapses (e.g., VM1/Ir92a ammonia; VA7l phenol; DL4 parasitoid odors) to known CSDn odor tuning. The significance statement frames this pair as a model for individual modulatory-neuron wiring.
summaries.advanced: This is light-microscopy/anatomical connectivity (GRASP-style and active-zone counts as described), not a dense EM antennal-lobe connectome. ‘Do not synapse upon ORNs’ is the authors’ anatomical conclusion. Heterogeneity is across glomeruli for this identified pair, not a claim about all serotonergic nuclei. Male/female sampling is not specified in the supplied extract.

plain_language_summary: Brain chemicals that change mood-like states are often imagined as a sprinkler system. In the fly nose, two serotonin cells both listen to and speak to specific odor channels, not uniformly.

ocar.opportunity: Anatomical EM cannot yet census synapses in large vertebrate populations. Inferring functional connectivity from activity could complement those maps if false positives from common input can be controlled.
ocar.challenge: Statistical connectomics still misreads correlated unconnected neurons; methods must be validated before in vivo whole-brain application.
ocar.action: Dunn and Koo, on bioRxiv (2017), combine residual convolutional networks with model-free partial correlation coefficients and evaluate on synthetic ChaLearn/Kaggle Connectomics data.
ocar.resolution: RCNN+PC is reported to outperform published methods on competition graphs, with over 90% precision at 1% recall on validation sets. The authors suggest that applying the model to larval zebrafish whole-brain imaging could recover on the order of 10^6 synaptic connections at a 10% false-discovery rate. Table 1 in the extract lists AUC-ROC/PR values with RCNN+PC as the benchmark on five networks.
ocar.future_work: The summary stresses that constraints and pitfalls must be understood before conservative use on real data; zebrafish application is a projection, not a result of this preprint.

summaries.beginner: Watching neurons fire together is cheaper than photographing every synapse, but it is easy to mistake coincidence for a real connection. This preprint trains a deep net on fake circuits to get better at guessing the real wires.
summaries.intermediate: Dunn and Koo (bioRxiv, 2017) improve deep functional-connectomics inference by pairing residual CNNs with partial correlation coefficients. On synthetic ChaLearn Connectomics (Kaggle) graphs, RCNN+PC sets the listed ROC/PR benchmarks in their Table 1 and is said to exceed 90% precision at 1% recall on validation data. They argue the approach should generalize across connection probabilities and parallelize on GPUs. A suggested future use is larval zebrafish whole-brain calcium imaging, where they estimate on the order of 10^6 recoverable connections at 10% FDR. False-positive motif analysis (common input, polysynaptic, reciprocal) appears in Table 2.
summaries.advanced: All quantitative scores are on synthetic ChaLearn data, not zebrafish recordings. The 10^6-connection / 10% FDR figure is an extrapolation stated as ‘this suggests that future application… could’. ‘Over 90% precision at 1% recall’ is the abstract’s validation claim. Uncertified preprint. Catalog organism tag zebrafish reflects that projection, not an experiment in the paper.

plain_language_summary: Watching neurons fire together is cheaper than photographing every synapse, but it is easy to mistake coincidence for a real connection. This preprint trains a deep net on fake circuits to get better at guessing the real wires.

ocar.opportunity: Spinally projecting RVLM neurons generate vasomotor tone and are thought to collect inputs from the entire neuraxis. A monosynaptic map in atlas coordinates would show which levels actually contact them.
ocar.challenge: Their ongoing activity’s sources remain unresolved; conventional tracing is hard to quantify and share in a common volume.
ocar.action: Dempsey, Le, Turner, Bokiniec, Ramadas, Bjaalie, Menuet, Neve, Allen, Goodchild, and McMullan, in Frontiers in Neural Circuits (2017), infect bulbospinal rat RVLM neurons with recombinant rabies that labels monosynaptic inputs, then place those cells in an MRI volumetric atlas with a custom alignment tool.
ocar.resolution: Most inputs are in the brainstem (88–94% in the abstract), including putative respiratory neurons in pre-Bötzinger and the post-inspiratory complex, plus a previously unrecognized input ventral to nucleus prepositus hypoglossi. Suprapontine inputs (PVN, lateral hypothalamus, PAG, superior colliculus) are sparse; cortex and amygdala are almost absent. Discussion adds ~14% of inputs in the RVLM region, ~30% within 1 mm of the epicenter, and about 3% each from forebrain and midbrain.
ocar.future_work: The authors note that targeting T2-projecting sympathetic premotor neurons may miss cortical/limbic input to other RVLM cells, and that disynaptic routes remain possible. The atlas pipeline is offered for sharing full datasets.

summaries.beginner: The brainstem cells that keep blood pressure up were thought to hear from the whole brain. A viral map in the rat finds that almost all of their direct incoming wires stay in the brainstem.
summaries.intermediate: Dempsey and colleagues (Frontiers in Neural Circuits, 2017) map monosynaptic inputs to bulbospinal RVLM sympathetic premotor neurons in rat with genetically restricted rabies and an MRI-based volumetric atlas. Abstract: 88–94% of inputs lie in the brainstem, including putative respiratory neurons in pre-Bötzinger and the post-inspiratory complex, plus a substantial previously unrecognized input just ventral to nucleus prepositus hypoglossi. Suprapontine autonomic nuclei contribute sparsely; cortex and amygdala almost not at all. Discussion: ~14% of input neurons in the RVLM region, ~30% within 1 mm, ~3% forebrain, ~3% midbrain. The authors argue this pattern fits little direct role in acute psychological stress, with possible indirect relays.
summaries.advanced: Rabies monosynaptic tracing, not EM. Percentages 88–94% (abstract) and 14%/30%/3%/3% (discussion) are those stated; they sum inputs across experiments/atlas segments. Almost no cortex/amygdala is a tracing result for T2-projecting targets, which the authors themselves qualify. Distance is argued not to explain missing long-range labels. Open-access Frontiers PDF.

plain_language_summary: The brainstem cells that keep blood pressure up were thought to hear from the whole brain. A viral map in the rat finds that almost all of their direct incoming wires stay in the brainstem.

ocar.opportunity: A century after D’Arcy Thompson’s On Growth and Form, experimental methods can watch anatomical brain networks change. Stated principles of connectome development would link space, time, disease, and individualized treatment.
ocar.challenge: How spatial and temporal factors shape healthy versus diseased connectomes, and how network structure relates to function, remains incompletely specified.
ocar.action: Kaiser, in Trends in Cognitive Sciences (2017), as described in the catalog abstract, outlines potential principles of connectome development and reviews how spatial and temporal factors shape networks in health and disease.
ocar.resolution: The abstract argues that understanding developmental origins of brain disease in individuals will matter for personalized treatment, and that longitudinal studies, experimentally derived parameters of connection formation, and biologically realistic computational models are needed to link development, structure, and function.
ocar.future_work: Those methodological needs are the paper’s stated agenda; details beyond the abstract cannot be taken from the mismatched PDF extract.

summaries.beginner: Brain wiring is not a finished photograph; it grows. This review asks what spatial and timing rules build healthy connection maps and how those rules fail in disease.
summaries.intermediate: Kaiser (Trends in Cognitive Sciences, 2017) reviews principles of connectome development at the centenary of D’Arcy Thompson’s On Growth and Form. According to the catalog abstract, the article covers spatial and temporal factors that shape anatomical brain networks in health and disease, and it argues that personalized treatment will require understanding developmental origins of brain disease in individuals. It calls for longitudinal studies, experimentally derived parameters of connection formation, and biologically realistic models linking development, structure, and function. Summaries follow the catalog abstract because the associated PDF extract is a different article.
summaries.advanced: The PDF text supplied with pdf_trust=ok is van Houtum et al., Schizophrenia Bulletin (2026), on fetal head growth and head circumference at birth in children of women with psychotic disorders versus population controls, not Kaiser’s TICS review. Numbers and claims above are taken only from the catalog abstract. Independent reading of the Trends in Cognitive Sciences paper is required for mechanisms, figures, and cited developmental studies.

plain_language_summary: Brain wiring is not a finished photograph; it grows. This review asks what spatial and timing rules build healthy connection maps and how those rules fail in disease.

ocar.opportunity: Connectome plus biophysics define a dynome that is too large to explore by exhaustive stimulation. A live graph that can be poked, ablated, and rewound would let hypotheses about function be tested in seconds.
ocar.challenge: Batch simulation of many stimulus patterns yields huge unlabeled time series; empirical search for meaningful stimulations is slow.
ocar.action: Kim, Leahy, and Shlizerman, in Frontiers in Computational Neuroscience (2019; catalogued as a 2017 bioRxiv record), present Neural Interactome, a cross-platform framework that visualizes graph structure together with simulated or recorded neural dynamics, with stimulation, ablation, zoom, review, and preset recording.
ocar.resolution: Implemented on a C. elegans nervous-system model with resolved connectome and dynamics, the tool is used to inspect locomotion-related patterns, revisit experimental touch-response circuits, and explore untested stimulation/ablation scenarios. The design is intended to swap in other connectivity and neuron models.
ocar.future_work: Planned extensions named in the extract include GPU integration for larger nets, connecting the neural model to musculature/body movement, and applying the same UI to other biological or artificial networks.

summaries.beginner: A wiring diagram sits still; the interesting part is watching it run. This software shows the worm’s nerve net as a live graph you can stimulate or snip, the way an experimenter would.
summaries.intermediate: Kim, Leahy, and Shlizerman (Frontiers in Computational Neuroscience, 2019) introduce Neural Interactome, combining graph visualization with real-time simulation (or playback of recorded traces). Users apply stimuli, ablate neurons, zoom to single cells, and review activity backward. They demonstrate it on a C. elegans model whose connectome and dynamics are specified, reproducing aspects of locomotion and touch-response exploration and proposing untested scenarios. Catalog metadata list year 2017 and journal bioRxiv; the PDF is the 2019 Frontiers methods paper with the same title and authors.
summaries.advanced: This is interactive simulation software, not new EM. Dynamics come from an existing computational model (279 neurons appear in an equation caption in the extract). Claims about discovering patterns ‘within seconds’ are qualitative. GPU acceleration and body coupling are future work. Open-access Frontiers PDF.

plain_language_summary: A wiring diagram sits still; the interesting part is watching it run. This software shows the worm’s nerve net as a live graph you can stimulate or snip, the way an experimenter would.

ocar.opportunity: Larval Drosophila odor-taste learning is cheap, genetically tractable, and about to sit beside a complete synaptic connectome. A classroom-ready manual would widen who can run the assay.
ocar.challenge: Newcomers lacked a sufficiently detailed, multilingual, hands-on protocol with scoring sheets.
ocar.action: Michels, Saumweber, Biernacki, Thum, Glasgow, Schleyer, Chen, Eschbach, Stocker, Toshima, Tanimura, Louis, Arias-Gil, Marescotti, Benfenati, and Gerber, in Frontiers in Behavioral Neuroscience (2017), publish an illustrated manual for Pavlovian odor-reward learning in maggots, with English, German, French, Japanese, Spanish, and Italian versions plus data-analysis tables.
ocar.resolution: The paradigm is described as robust enough for teaching and already adopted by multiple labs. Combined with single-cell transgenes and the forthcoming larval/adult connectome, it is framed as a bridge from behaviour to circuit to genes, including translational biomedicine via shared genetics with humans.
ocar.future_work: The paper is a methods/teaching resource; scientific extensions depend on users applying the protocol rather than new data herein.

summaries.beginner: Fruit-fly maggots can learn that a smell predicts a taste reward, using a setup simple enough for a classroom. This paper is the how-to guide, in several languages, so more people can run the experiment.
summaries.intermediate: Michels and colleagues (Frontiers in Behavioral Neuroscience, 2017) provide a hands-on, illustrated manual for Pavlovian odor-reward (odor-taste) learning in larval Drosophila. They emphasize low cost, robustness, scoring and analysis sheets, brief scientific context, and multilingual supplements (English, German, French, Japanese, Spanish, Italian). The assay is positioned for behavioural neurogenetics, experimental psychology, teaching, and translational work, and is explicitly linked to the forthcoming complete synaptic connectome and cell-specific transgenes. It is a protocol paper, not a connectomic reconstruction.
summaries.advanced: No new circuit map or learning-rate numbers are in the extract; the contribution is documentation. ‘Upcoming total synaptic connectome’ is the 2017 framing. Author list on the PDF is longer than the catalog abbreviation. Open-access Frontiers methods article.

plain_language_summary: Fruit-fly maggots can learn that a smell predicts a taste reward, using a setup simple enough for a classroom. This paper is the how-to guide, in several languages, so more people can run the experiment.

ocar.opportunity: Volume-EM reconstructions supply neuron geometry that compartmental simulators such as NEURON are built to run. Closing that loop would test whether extracted circuits reproduce known computations.
ocar.challenge: EM does not give synapse signs or channel models; fully detailed meshes are extremely slow to simulate.
ocar.action: Gornet and Scheffer, on bioRxiv (2017), take Drosophila motion-detection neurons, attach approximate synapses from known/estimated function, simulate direction selectivity in T4, then coarsen geometry from a full compartment model down to a single node.
ocar.resolution: They reproduce T4 direction selectivity, verifying extraction plus simulation. Simplified models, including a lumped single-node neuron, give nearly the same computation. The full model is given as 200,000 nodes, a reduced model 28,000, and a node model 187; the single-node model is at least four orders of magnitude faster. Biologically, they confirm Gruntman that dendritic computation is not required for this detector.
ocar.future_work: Gap junctions and neuromodulators are named as missing. The authors expect reduction to matter more as larger fly EM volumes arrive; reducing every neuron to a point will not always suffice for larger cells.

summaries.beginner: Once a fly neuron’s shape is traced from electron microscopy, you can try to run it as a simulation. This preprint shows that a simple blob model, not a full 3-D tree, is enough for a famous motion-detecting cell.
summaries.intermediate: Gornet and Scheffer (bioRxiv, 2017) simulate EM-extracted Drosophila medulla neurons in the motion-detection pathway. Because synapse physiology is unavailable from EM, they insert approximate synapses with estimated signs and recover T4 direction selectivity. They then compare a fully detailed compartment model (200,000 nodes) with a reduced branched model (28,000) and a single-node model (187). The lumped model is at least 10^4 times faster and still reproduces the main detector operation, supporting Gruntman et al. that dendritic computation is not required. They argue connectivity matters more than detailed shape for these medulla neurons.
summaries.advanced: bioRxiv preprint. Synapse models are approximate, not measured from the EM volume. Node counts and the four-orders-of-magnitude runtime claim are from the extract (full-model times are underestimates because runs were killed after one day). Confirmation of Gruntman is for this T4 on-pathway case. Not a claim about all fly neurons.

plain_language_summary: Once a fly neuron’s shape is traced from electron microscopy, you can try to run it as a simulation. This preprint shows that a simple blob model, not a full 3-D tree, is enough for a famous motion-detecting cell.

ocar.opportunity: Graphs from connectomes and social networks need inferential statistics analogous to Euclidean data: embeddings, consistency, asymptotic normality, and hypothesis tests.
ocar.challenge: Independent-edge models that are both tractable and flexible enough to approximate block models and latent-position graphs are scarce; spectral methods need a unified theory.
ocar.action: Athreya, Fishkind, Tang, Priebe, Park, Vogelstein, Levin, Lyzinski, Qin, and Sussman, in a 2017 Journal of Machine Learning Research / arXiv survey, review random dot product graphs and inference based on adjacency and Laplacian spectral embeddings.
ocar.resolution: They summarize consistency and asymptotic normality of those embeddings, their use in single- and multi-sample graph hypothesis tests, and applications including community detection in social networks and exploratory analysis of the Drosophila connectome for functional and biologically relevant structure. Open problems in spectral graph inference are outlined.
ocar.future_work: The survey’s later pages in the extract are technical proofs (e.g., Laplacian embedding error bounds); remaining open problems are flagged rather than solved here.

summaries.beginner: A brain wiring diagram is a giant network, and networks need statistics just as tables of numbers do. This survey explains a model that turns a network into points in space so you can test and cluster them.
summaries.intermediate: Athreya and colleagues (JMLR / arXiv:1709.05454, 2017) survey random dot product graphs (RDPGs) as a tractable independent-edge model spanning stochastic block models to latent-position graphs. The paradigm centers on adjacency and Laplacian spectral embeddings, with results on consistency and asymptotic normality and on building graph hypothesis tests. Applications mentioned include large social-network community detection/classification and exploratory analysis of the Drosophila connectome. The extract’s visible tail is linear-algebraic error bounds (e.g., Frobenius residuals of order O(n^{-1}) with high probability).
summaries.advanced: This is a statistical survey, not an EM methods paper. Drosophila connectome use is an application cited in the abstract, not a new reconstruction. Catalog uuid equals work_id (no DOI). The supplied extract is truncated deep in proofs; biological findings should be read from the application section of the full survey, not invented from the proof pages.

plain_language_summary: A brain wiring diagram is a giant network, and networks need statistics just as tables of numbers do. This survey explains a model that turns a network into points in space so you can test and cluster them.

ocar.opportunity: Rich-club organization—hubs densely interconnected with each other—has been reported from human MRI down to C. elegans. A microscale electrophysiology paper could test whether the same architecture carries most information flow among neurons.
ocar.challenge: Macroscale rich clubs do not automatically imply the same phenomenon at single-neuron effective connectivity, and directionality of information flow is easy to confound.
ocar.action: Pedersen and Omidvarnia, in a Journal of Neuroscience Journal Club (2016), review Nigam et al. (2016) on rich-club architecture in neuronal networks, covering in vitro organotypic and in vivo microelectrode effective-connectivity analyses.
ocar.resolution: They highlight Nigam et al.’s finding that a rich club carries a high percentage (~70%) of incoming and outgoing information flow, discuss metrics such as transfer entropy and dynamic importance, and point to Fulcher and Fornito’s mesoscale mouse connectome as bridging macro- and microscale rich clubs, including metabolic-gene associations at hub nodes.
ocar.future_work: They suggest multivariate information-transfer criteria as a path for neuronal rich-club research. The Journal Club itself presents no new data.

summaries.beginner: Some brain regions are like busy train stations that also have extra tracks to each other. This short student/postdoc commentary explains a study that found the same ‘rich club’ among individual neurons and argues most messages travel through it.
summaries.intermediate: Pedersen and Omidvarnia (Journal of Neuroscience, 2016) write a Journal Club on Nigam et al. (2016). After placing rich clubs at macro-, meso-, and microscales (human, newborn, macaque, C. elegans, mouse hippocampus), they summarize Nigam’s effective-connectivity analysis in organotypic cultures and in vivo arrays, including a reported ~70% of incoming and outgoing information flow through the rich club. They discuss directional flow, network drive, and spurious delayed connections as methodological issues. They close by citing Fulcher and Fornito (2016) on a mesoscale mouse connectome in which rich-club nodes associate with metabolic-regulation genes.
summaries.advanced: This is a two-page Journal Club, not original connectomics. The ~70% figure is attributed to Nigam et al. as presented here. Catalog abstract is truncated. PMC PDF. Do not treat commentary citations as new measurements.

plain_language_summary: Some brain regions are like busy train stations that also have extra tracks to each other. This short student/postdoc commentary explains a study that found the same ‘rich club’ among individual neurons and argues most messages travel through it.

ocar.opportunity: Multimodal 3-D light and electron microscopy are more accessible, but processing, visualization, and quantitative analysis of large volumes remain a bottleneck, especially versus costly commercial packages.
ocar.challenge: Existing freeware tools are fragmented; labs need an open, scriptable segmentation workbench with interpolation, classifiers, and microscopy-aware I/O.
ocar.action: Belevich, Joensuu, Kumar, Vihinen, and Jokitalo, in PLoS Biology (2016), introduce Microscopy Image Browser (MIB), a high-performance open-source package for segmentation and image processing of multidimensional datasets, with plug-in extensibility and tutorials.
ocar.resolution: They demonstrate tools (brush, ball, magic wand, line tracker, interpolation, random forest, watershed, thresholding) on light- and electron-microscopy examples including lipid droplets, Golgi, ER, microtubules, nuclear envelope, mitochondria, and serial-block-face EM. The software is free from a dedicated site and customizable in MATLAB.
ocar.future_work: Community plug-ins and new modalities are invited; MIB is infrastructure rather than a biological result.

summaries.beginner: 3-D microscope movies pile up faster than people can outline the objects inside them. This free program gives biologists a workbench to paint, interpolate, and measure cells and organelles in those volumes.
summaries.intermediate: Belevich and colleagues (PLoS Biology, 2016) present Microscopy Image Browser, an open-source MATLAB environment for processing and segmenting multidimensional light- and electron-microscopy data. Features shown include basic 3-D painting tools, superpixels, interpolation, a random-forest classifier, and watershed, with video tutorials on lipid droplets, Golgi, ER, microtubules, nuclei, and mitochondria. The authors contrast MIB with commercial Amira/Imaris and with Fiji, IMOD, ilastik, and related freeware. Plug-ins can be added for lab-specific needs.
summaries.advanced: This is a software/community-page paper. No single accuracy benchmark versus other segmenters is in the extract. Examples include SB-EM and electron tomography specimen acknowledgments. License/download details are on the authors’ site rather than fully quoted here.

plain_language_summary: 3-D microscope movies pile up faster than people can outline the objects inside them. This free program gives biologists a workbench to paint, interpolate, and measure cells and organelles in those volumes.

ocar.opportunity: Anatomical and functional connectomes are becoming high-resolution, but the molecular tags that make synapses specific and physiologically distinct are still hard to list at circuit scale.
ocar.challenge: Genetic tests of chemoaffinity have power and limits; they rarely yield a complete molecular synaptic connectome.
ocar.action: Schreiner, Savas, Herzog, Brose, and de Wit, in Current Opinion in Neurobiology (2017 version of a 2016 paper), review genetic approaches to synaptic connectivity and function and discuss proteomic and proximity-labeling methods as a path to a molecular synaptic connectome underlying the neural connectome.
ocar.resolution: They argue that proximity labeling, targeted to specific neurons or even synapses, plus shotgun and quantitative mass spectrometry, can define synapse-type proteomes. Combined with combinatorial genetics, that molecular map is presented as the way to explain anatomical and functional wiring.
ocar.future_work: The conclusion treats these tools as promising rather than as a completed molecular connectome; coverage is explicitly limited by the Current Opinion format.
