summaries.beginner: Knowing which cells touch is not the same as knowing which molecular Velcro made that contact. This review sketches how protein-labeling chemistry could catalog the ingredients of specific synapses.
summaries.intermediate: Schreiner, Savas, Herzog, Brose, and de Wit (Current Opinion in Neurobiology, 2017; DOI 2016) review paths toward molecular connectomics. After noting that anatomical/functional maps now outrun mechanistic explanation, they discuss limits of genetic analysis of synaptic specificity and highlight proximity-labeling proteomics (down to specific synapses) plus evolving mass spectrometry. The stated goal is a molecular synaptic connectome that accounts for anatomical and functional connectivity. The extract is an NIHMS author manuscript.
summaries.advanced: This is a short opinion/review, not new proteomic data. Sperry’s chemoaffinity hypothesis is background. No protein lists or synapse counts are in the extract. Catalog year 2016; published form February 2017 (volume 42, pages 102–110) as given on the manuscript header.

plain_language_summary: Knowing which cells touch is not the same as knowing which molecular Velcro made that contact. This review sketches how protein-labeling chemistry could catalog the ingredients of specific synapses.

ocar.opportunity: Connectomics and other neuroanatomy need banked brains that keep traceable processes and crisp synapses over long storage, at a scale that perfusion can reach (rabbit to pig).
ocar.challenge: Ice-free long-term storage and excellent ultrastructure have been hard to combine; many banking methods do not scale by perfusion or do not allow cryoprotectant washout for later assays.
ocar.action: McIntyre and Fahy, in Cryobiology (2015), as described in the catalog abstract, introduce aldehyde-stabilized cryopreservation (ASC): glutaraldehyde perfusion fixation of rabbit and pig brains, slow perfusion to 65% w/v ethylene glycol, vitrification at −135 °C, rewarming, and cryoprotectant removal by perfusion or slice diffusion.
ocar.resolution: The abstract reports uniformly excellent preservation on multi-region electron microscopy and on FIB-SEM of selected volumes: processes easily traceable and synapses crisp in both species. Advantages claimed: perfusion scaling, vitrification for long-term ultrastructural stability, and a washable, still-perfusable aldehyde-fixed brain for diverse assays.
ocar.future_work: Independent reading of the Cryobiology paper is required for methods detail, quantification, and limits; the mismatched PDF cannot supply them.

summaries.beginner: Brain maps need tissue that can sit on a shelf without ice damage and still show clean synapses. This paper’s abstract describes fixing rabbit and pig brains, filling them with antifreeze, and glassifying them for long-term storage.
summaries.intermediate: McIntyre and Fahy (Cryobiology, 2015), according to the catalog abstract, perfuse-fix rabbit and pig brains with a glutaraldehyde-based fixative, ramp ethylene glycol to 65% w/v, vitrify at −135 °C, then rewarm and remove cryoprotectant by perfusion or diffusion from slices. They evaluate preservation by electron microscopy across regions and by FIB-SEM of selected volumes, reporting uniformly excellent, traceable processes and crisp synapses in both species. ASC is framed as a scalable brain-banking method for connectomics. Summaries follow the catalog abstract because the associated PDF extract is a different article.
summaries.advanced: The PDF text supplied with pdf_trust=ok is Ströh, Hammerschmith, Tank, Seung, and Wanner, eLife (2022), on in situ X-ray-assisted electron-microscopy staining of large samples, not McIntyre and Fahy’s aldehyde-stabilized cryopreservation. Numbers and claims above (65% w/v ethylene glycol, −135 °C, rabbit and pig, FIB-SEM) are taken only from the catalog abstract. Independent reading of the Cryobiology paper is required for methods, quantification, and figures.

plain_language_summary: Brain maps need tissue that can sit on a shelf without ice damage and still show clean synapses. This paper’s abstract describes fixing rabbit and pig brains, filling them with antifreeze, and glassifying them for long-term storage.
